notes: M2.5 Nigeria human semantic review. Hardening I–III rows HCR-NG-001..044 remain frozen. Hardening IV (NG-B4) rows HCR-NG-045..057 close CC-NG-REG-001..013. Classification only: not adopted, not project-claim statuses, not a publication flip. Current-rule floating/managed-float taxonomy and 'significant exchange controls' remain not established. Historical managed-float candidates remain period-scoped.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals into Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigeria Customs Service.
reviews.rationale: Entry limb of MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) is supported. Declared bounded_normalization splits the statutory 'in or out of Nigeria' phrase into an atomic entry candidate and preserves the statutory operator 'in excess of' (>). This establishes a declaration obligation only; it does not establish a physical carriage ceiling.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals out of Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigeria Customs Service.
reviews.rationale: Exit limb of MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) is supported independently of the entry candidate. Statutory operator remains 'in excess of' (>). Exit declaration is established; a general outbound carriage ceiling is not.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: False declaration or failure to make the required declaration to the Nigeria Customs Service is an offence that may lead on conviction to forfeiture of the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument, imprisonment for at least two years, or both.
reviews.reviewed_text: Any person who falsely declares or fails to make a declaration to the Nigeria Customs Service under section 12 of the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act commits an offence and is liable on conviction to forfeit the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument or to imprisonment for a term of at least two years or both.
reviews.rationale: As written, 'may lead' softens MLPPA 2022 s.3(5) liability wording. Bounded reviewed_text restores the statutory 'commits an offence and is liable on conviction' formulation and retains the FEMMPA s.12 cross-reference from the same excerpt. The omitted s.3(4) Customs-to-CBN/Unit reporting chain remains a separate proposition and is not adopted here.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The reviewed official CBN guidance states that the declaration rule for cash or negotiable instruments above US$10,000 does not itself prohibit genuinely owned or obtained funds above that amount from being brought into Nigeria or taken outside the country.
reviews.rationale: Supported as a bounded negative reading of the CBN circular: the declaration rule itself is not a prohibition on genuinely owned funds above the threshold. The candidate already uses 'does not itself prohibit' and therefore does not claim unrestricted carriage, absence of other restrictions, or a without-limit absolute.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Where foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 is imported in cash and deposited into a domiciliary account with an authorised dealer, the account may only be withdrawn from in cash and that imported cash is exportable from Nigeria only in cash.
reviews.reviewed_text: Where a person imports foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent in cash and not by means of a bank draft, mail or telegraphic transfer and deposits the foreign currency in a domiciliary account with an authorised dealer, withdrawals from that account may be made only in cash, and that imported cash is exportable from Nigeria only in cash.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.21(1)-(2) is narrow. The original candidate omitted the cash-not-transfer condition in s.21(1). Bounded reviewed_text restores that condition from the same excerpt and keeps the rule limited to imported cash deposited in a domiciliary account. It must not be generalised into a universal outbound traveller rule, amount-declared-on-entry ceiling, or universal authorised-dealer-document requirement.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The importation and exportation of the naira remain prohibited except as permitted under guidelines issued from time to time by the Central Bank.
reviews.rationale: Direct restatement of FEMMPA 1995 s.14. Supported as the prohibition baseline only. Hardening I-B established that no current primary CBN guideline setting a live numeric traveller exception was pinned; therefore this candidate must not be read as establishing N10,000, N20,000, N100,000, or any other numeric exception.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Current Customs operational guidance uses a declaration trigger of US$10,000 or more, which conflicts with the statutory phrase in excess of US$10,000.
reviews.reviewed_text: Current Customs operational guidance on the e-currency declaration form uses a declaration trigger of US$10,000 or more / equal to or greater than US$10,000.
reviews.rationale: Special review closed. The direct NCS e-CDF excerpt supports only the operational >= trigger. The candidate's assertion that this 'conflicts with' the statute synthesises beyond that single excerpt. Bounded reviewed_text retains the Customs operational operator (>=) only. Dual-operator preservation against MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) (>) remains an I-B source-layer disposition and must not be flattened into one synthetic universal threshold in this candidate.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The earlier Foreign Exchange Act wording requiring declaration only when foreign currency exceeds US$5,000 is a legacy threshold retained for temporal audit and should not be used as the current border-cash rule while MLPPA 2022 is operative.
reviews.reviewed_text: FEMMPA 1995 section 12 states that foreign currency in excess of US$5,000 or its equivalent, whether being imported into or exported out of Nigeria, shall be declared on the prescribed form for reasons of statistics only. That older threshold wording is retained for temporal audit and must not drive the current border-cash declaration threshold while MLPPA 2022 section 3(3) uses in excess of US$10,000.
reviews.rationale: Special review closed. As written, the candidate compressed the FEMMPA s.12 text and asserted temporal supersession without restoring the statistical-declaration pinpoint. Bounded reviewed_text restores the s.12 statistical declaration wording and preserves the Hardening I temporal disposition that this older US$5,000 threshold must not drive current public declaration wording while MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) remains the operative AML/customs declaration text.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Any person may open, maintain and operate a domiciliary account designated in foreign currency with an Authorised Dealer.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(1) directly supports domiciliary-account opening with an Authorised Dealer. Supported as account-opening permission only. Does not establish unrestricted FX access, unrestricted international transfer, unrestricted physical FX holding, absence of KYC, or absence of all regulatory limits.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The foreign currency in which a domiciliary account may be opened, maintained and operated shall be any internationally convertible currency.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(2) directly supports internationally convertible currency denomination for domiciliary accounts. Currency rule only; not a transfer or holding entitlement.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Except as provided under any other enactment or law, a person making an application to open a domiciliary account under this Act shall not be obliged to disclose the source of the foreign currency sought to be deposited in the account.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(3) is supported with the statutory exception limb preserved: source disclosure is not obliged except as provided under any other enactment or law. Special review closed. Does not establish unrestricted funding or that KYC/AML source-of-funds checks never apply.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A person may open more than one domiciliary account under this Act designated in the same or different foreign currencies and at the same or in different banks.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(4) directly supports multiple domiciliary accounts in the same or different currencies and banks. Multiple-account permission only.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: An exporter of goods, including petroleum products, shall open and maintain a foreign currency domiciliary account into which may be retained foreign currency corresponding to the entire proceeds of the export concerned.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.19 directly supports the exporter-specific obligation to open and maintain a foreign-currency domiciliary account for export proceeds. Kept as a separate account class; not generalised to ordinary domiciliary accounts. FX Manual 2026 export-proceeds operational restrictions remain outside this candidate.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: For external and non-resident non-Nigerian customers, financial institutions shall satisfy themselves that the customer is permanently resident outside Nigeria, and the eligible classes for external accounts are embassies, high commissions, legations or consulates, their career and established members, and other international organisations recognised and accorded diplomatic status and their expatriate officials.
reviews.rationale: CBN CDD Regulations 2023 reg. 25(1)-(2) supported for external-account eligibility classes (diplomatic / international-organisation). Special review closed. Category-specific only; not a universal non-resident FCY entitlement.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The eligible classes to open non-resident accounts under the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations are overseas correspondence and examination bodies, foreign companies executing approved contracts in Nigeria, and foreign professional bodies.
reviews.rationale: CBN CDD Regulations 2023 reg. 25(4) supported for the three listed non-resident account eligible classes. Special review closed. Does not support 'all non-residents may open FCY accounts' or comparative freer-transfer wording.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: All accounts of Non-resident stipulated for the external-account and non-resident-account eligible classes shall, on completion of the contract or the applicant’s business in Nigeria, be closed and the balance on the account, if any, transferred to the customer’s account in country of residence, after proper documentation.
reviews.reviewed_text: All accounts of Non-resident stipulated in subregulations (2) and (4) of regulation 25 of the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations, 2023, shall, on completion of the contract or the applicant's business in Nigeria, be closed and the balance on the account, if any, transferred to the customer's account in country of residence, after proper documentation.
reviews.rationale: CDD reg. 25(7) closure rule is supported but the candidate compressed the subregulation cross-reference. Bounded reviewed_text restores the subregulation (2) and (4) pinpoint so closure remains limited to those eligible classes. Special review closed. Not a universal non-resident closure rule.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Where a customer wishes to open a domiciliary account or make a wholesale deposit by cash or inter-bank transfer, a financial institution shall obtain identification evidence appropriate to individuals, companies, or professional intermediaries, and where funding is by inter-bank transfer the institution shall satisfy itself that the transferring institution is regulated for ML, TF or PF prevention in its country of origin.
reviews.rationale: CBN CDD Regulations 2023 reg. 40 supported as bank identification / KYC for domiciliary opening or wholesale cash/inter-bank deposit. Special review closed. Explicit boundary: bank KYC / customer identification is not CBN prior regulatory approval to open a domiciliary account and does not recreate legacy 'CBN approval required' wording.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Effective 1 January 2025, eligible Non-Resident Nigerians may own a Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account or a Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account subject to meeting KYC requirements, without prejudice to Memorandum 17 of the CBN Foreign Exchange Manual (2018).
reviews.rationale: CBN 2025 NRNOA/NRNIA circular introduction supported for eligible Non-Resident Nigerians from 1 January 2025 subject to KYC, with the Memorandum 17 (2018) without-prejudice exception preserved. Special review closed. Not generalised to all non-residents, foreign nationals, foreign companies, or temporary visitors.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account enables Non-Resident Nigerians to remit their foreign earnings to Nigeria and manage funds in both foreign and local currencies; account holders may maintain both a foreign-currency account and/or a Naira account.
reviews.rationale: NRNOA purpose and dual-currency structure supported from the CBN framework excerpt. Special review closed. NRNOA-only; conversion and repatriation limbs remain in separate candidates.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account enables Non-Resident Nigerians to invest in assets in Nigeria in either foreign currency or local currency, and account holders may maintain both a foreign-currency account and/or a Naira account for that purpose.
reviews.rationale: NRNIA investment-purpose account class supported from the CBN framework excerpt. Special review closed. Distinct from NRNOA; not generalised beyond Non-Resident Nigerians.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: On 15 May 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria officially launched the Fourth Edition of its Foreign Exchange Manual.
reviews.rationale: CBN Reforms page launch statement for Foreign Exchange Manual Fourth Edition (15 May 2026) is supported as temporal meta only. Special review closed. Does not supply or resolve ordinary-vs-export domiciliary operational rules, Form A mechanics, or export cash-withdrawal restrictions; those remain unresolved pending a pinned Manual PDF.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: In cases that are not classified under the external-account or non-resident-account eligible classes in the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations, financial institutions shall refer to the Central Bank of Nigeria for clarification.
reviews.rationale: CDD reg. 25(8) clarification-referral rule supported for cases not classified under the external-account or non-resident-account eligible classes. Special review closed. Narrow referral only — not converted into 'all non-resident accounts require CBN approval'.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Balances in the foreign-currency account of a Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account can be fully repatriated out of Nigeria without restriction.
reviews.rationale: CBN NRNOA framework 1.4 directly states FCY balances can be fully repatriated out of Nigeria without restriction. Supported with subject limited to NRNOA foreign-currency account balances. Special review closed. Not expanded to all non-resident accounts, all FCY accounts, all capital or investment funds, or resident accounts.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account holders may maintain a Naira account with funds remitted directly from offshore or convertible from a foreign-currency account at prevailing exchange rates through authorised dealers.
reviews.rationale: CBN NRNOA framework currency/conversion limb supported: Naira account funded from offshore remittance or conversion from FCY via authorised dealers. Funding-channel rule for NRNOA only; not a general unrestricted-funding proposition and not an FX Manual 2026 local-deposit schedule.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The Central Bank may appoint, as an Authorised Dealer or Authorised Buyer of foreign currency, any bank or non-banking corporate organisation which shows evidence of adequate resources and capacity to operate under the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, subject to terms and conditions in the letter of appointment.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.5(1)-(2) appointment architecture supported: CBN may appoint Authorised Dealers or Authorised Buyers (bank or non-banking corporate) subject to letter-of-appointment terms. Special review closed. Establishes distinct statutory participant classes only — not that every FX transaction is bank-only, and not that BDCs are Authorised Dealers.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Transactions in the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market are between the public and Authorised Dealers, among Authorised Dealers, and between Authorised Dealers and Authorised Buyers, and shall be as prescribed from time to time by the Central Bank.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.7(1)-(2) Market counterparty channels supported: public↔Authorised Dealer, Authorised Dealer↔Authorised Dealer, and Authorised Dealer↔Authorised Buyer, as prescribed by the Central Bank. Special review closed. Statutory Market architecture only — not a proof that every retail NFEM flow, every EFEMS participant class, or every BDC transaction is identical to these Market limbs.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The rate at which each transaction in the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market shall be executed shall be the rate mutually agreed between the applicant purchaser and the Authorised Dealer or Authorised Buyer concerned.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.9 transaction-execution rate rule supported: rate mutually agreed between applicant purchaser and the Authorised Dealer or Authorised Buyer concerned. Special review closed. Transaction-level Market pricing mechanic only — does not establish an NG-B4 free-floating / managed / market-determined exchange-rate-regime classification.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Except where a transaction is prohibited by law and subject to section 11(b), any transaction adequately supported by appropriate documentation shall be an eligible transaction for the purchase of foreign exchange in the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.10 documentation-backed Market eligibility supported, with s.11(b) exception preserved: appropriate documentation makes a non-prohibited transaction eligible for Market FX purchase. Special review closed. Documentation ≠ Form M for every goods import, ≠ Form A for every service import, ≠ CBN prior approval, and ≠ a uniform documentary package. Current Form M/A schedules remain unpinned.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Nothing in the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act shall be construed as permitting any unrestrained or general dealing in foreign currencies on terms inconsistent with that Act, or as permitting Market transactions relating to goods, services or items absolutely prohibited by any enactment or law.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.11(a)-(b) construction boundaries supported: the Act does not permit unrestrained dealing inconsistent with its terms, and does not permit Market transactions in absolutely prohibited goods/services/items. Special review closed. Statutory anti-unrestrained-dealing and prohibited-items boundary only — not a general characterization that Nigerian FX is tightly controlled, that all transactions are restricted, or that FX availability is regulated.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Any foreign currency purchased from the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market may be repatriated from Nigeria and shall not be subject to any further approval.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.13 supported with negative-claim discipline: foreign currency purchased from the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market may be repatriated and shall not be subject to any further approval. Special review closed. Prerequisite 'purchased from the Market' is retained. Does not establish that no CBN approval is ever required, that business FX generally needs no approval, that all capital repatriation is approval-free, or that all outward remittances are approval-free.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Any person may invest in any enterprise or security with foreign currency or capital imported into Nigeria through an Authorised Dealer by telegraphic transfer, cheques or other negotiable instruments and converted into the naira in the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market in accordance with the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.15(1) inward investment channel supported: foreign currency/capital imported through an Authorised Dealer and converted into naira in the Market. Special review closed. Investment-entry mechanism only — not prior CBN permission to invest as a general approval gate, and not proof that all inward business FX is investment capital.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The Authorised Dealer through which foreign currency or capital for an investment under section 15(1) is imported shall, within 24 hours of the importation, issue a Certificate of Capital Importation to the investor and shall, within 48 hours thereafter, make returns to the Central Bank.
reviews.reviewed_text: The Authorised Dealer through which the foreign currency or capital for an investment under section 15(1) is imported shall, within 24 hours of the importation, issue a Certificate of Capital Importation to the investor and shall, within 48 hours thereafter, make returns to the Central Bank giving such information as the Central Bank may, from time to time, require.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.15(2) CCI issuance and AD returns supported. Bounded reviewed_text restores the statutory returns limb 'giving such information as the Central Bank may, from time to time, require,' omitted from candidate_text. Special review closed. CCI is a capital-importation certification/reporting mechanism — not prior CBN permission to invest and not a general approval requirement for all inward FX.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Foreign currency imported into Nigeria and invested in an enterprise under section 15(1) is guaranteed unconditional transferability, through an Authorised Dealer in freely convertible currency, of dividends or profits (net of taxes) attributable to the investment.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.15(4)(a) supported: unconditional transferability through an Authorised Dealer in freely convertible currency of dividends or profits (net of taxes) attributable to the qualifying s.15(1) investment. Statutory word 'unconditional' retained within investment/category/AD scope. Special review closed. Not expanded to all Nigerian business funds or free transferability outside the investment context.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Foreign currency imported into Nigeria and invested in an enterprise under section 15(1) is guaranteed unconditional transferability, through an Authorised Dealer in freely convertible currency, of payments in respect of loan servicing where a foreign loan has been obtained.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.15(4)(b) supported: unconditional transferability through an Authorised Dealer of payments in respect of loan servicing where a foreign loan has been obtained, for qualifying s.15(1) investment foreign currency. Special review closed. Term 'loan servicing' preserved — not rewritten as independently universal principal-and-interest transferability. Separate principal-vs-interest schedule remains not established.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Foreign currency imported into Nigeria and invested in an enterprise under section 15(1) is guaranteed unconditional transferability, through an Authorised Dealer in freely convertible currency, of the remittance of proceeds (net of all taxes) and other obligations in the event of sale or liquidation of the enterprise or any interest attributable to the investment.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.15(4)(c) supported: unconditional transferability through an Authorised Dealer of remittance of proceeds (net of all taxes) and other obligations on sale or liquidation of the enterprise or attributable interest, for qualifying s.15(1) investment foreign currency. Special review closed. Investment capital/liquidation limb only — not a general statement that all capital repatriation requires (or never requires) CBN approval, and not free transferability of all business funds.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: An Authorised Dealer shall communicate a section 15(4) repatriation to the Central Bank within fourteen days of the repatriation, and the Central Bank shall furnish the same to the Minister monthly for information and statistical purposes only.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.15(5) Authorised Dealer repatriation-reporting obligation supported: AD communicates a s.15(4) repatriation to CBN within fourteen days; CBN furnishes to the Minister monthly for information and statistical purposes only. Special review closed. Reporting ≠ prior CBN approval. Does not convert transferability rights into approval gates.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: An Authorised Dealer and Authorised Buyer appointed under the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act shall submit to the Central Bank, at intervals and in forms the Central Bank may prescribe by circulars and guidelines, returns of activities in the Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.16(1) Market activity returns supported for appointed Authorised Dealers and Authorised Buyers submitting returns to CBN in prescribed forms/intervals. Institutional reporting claim only — does not characterize the customer's transaction as requiring individual CBN permission.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A person may export goods or services from Nigeria if the goods or services are not prohibited by law in Nigeria, payment is made by letter of credit or any other internationally acceptable mode of payment, and the payment amount represents a fair return for the goods or services.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.27 export permission conditions supported: non-prohibited goods/services; payment by letter of credit or other internationally acceptable mode; payment amount representing a fair return. Special review closed. Export payment-mode mechanics only — does not manufacture the unresolved full export documentary schedule. Distinct from Hardening II exporter-domiciliary retention claim NG-ACC-05 / CC-NG-ACC-005; does not duplicate that account proposition.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Eligible transactions at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, including FX applications for medical needs, school fees, business travel allowance/personal travel allowance, and SME transactions, are permissible at the NFEM and processed by Deposit Money Banks.
reviews.reviewed_text: All eligible transactions such as FX applications for Medical Needs, School Fees, Business Travel Allowance/ Personal Travel Allowance (BTA/PTA), and Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) transactions are permissible at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and processed by the Deposit Money Banks.
reviews.rationale: CBN FX Management page NFEM/DMB processing limb supported. Bounded reviewed_text restores the source 'such as' framing for the listed eligible classes instead of candidate 'including,' reducing overbreadth risk. Special review closed. DMB channel for stated eligible NFEM classes only — not that all imports are automatically eligible, not that documentation disappeared, and not an NG-B4 regime label.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The Central Bank permitted accessibility of foreign exchange in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market for 43 items previously restricted by the 2015 circular TED/FEM/FPC/GEN/01/010 and its addendums.
reviews.rationale: CBN FX Management page temporal restoration claim supported: accessibility of FX in the NFEM was permitted for 43 items previously restricted by TED/FEM/FPC/GEN/01/010 (2015) and addendums. Special review closed. Current/temporal operating claim for those items only — not unrestricted NFEM access for all imports, not automatic eligibility for every import, and not disappearance of documentation requirements.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Authorised Dealers use the Electronic Foreign Exchange Matching System to place buy and sell orders for foreign exchange transactions in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, and Authorised Dealer Banks transition to EFEMS for interbank FX transactions.
reviews.reviewed_text: Authorised Dealers use the Electronic Foreign Exchange Matching System (EFEMS) to place buy and sell orders for foreign exchange transactions in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, and Authorised Dealer Banks use EFEMS for interbank FX transactions.
reviews.rationale: CBN EFEMS FAQ Authorised Dealer order-placement / interbank use supported. Bounded reviewed_text keeps the AD/ADB EFEMS role while removing transitional 'will transition from Refinitiv FXT' implementation narrative that is not needed for the standing institutional-channel proposition. Special review closed. Interbank/electronic infrastructure ≠ customer FX entitlement or automatic eligibility.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: EFEMS participants include all authorised dealer banks licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria and other participants who have secured CBN approval to access the EFEMS platform and execute agreements with the platform provider.
reviews.rationale: CBN Reforms page EFEMS participant-class description supported: authorised dealer banks licensed by CBN and other participants with CBN approval to access EFEMS and agreements with the platform provider. Special review closed. Participant-class architecture only — not proof that every CBN-approved EFEMS participant may perform every retail/customer FX transaction.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Duly licensed Bureau De Change operators are permitted to access foreign exchange through any Authorised Dealer of their choice at prevailing market rates, and Authorised Dealers must conduct complete KYC and due diligence checks on BDC clients.
reviews.rationale: CBN Reforms page BDC-via-AD access description supported: duly licensed BDCs may access FX through any Authorised Dealer at prevailing market rates, with AD KYC/due diligence on BDC clients. Special review closed. Preserves BDC as a distinct licensed class and the exact access-via-AD relationship. Does not equate BDC with Authorised Dealer, does not authorise BDCs for every business FX transaction, and does not revive bank-only universality.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The Central Bank of Nigeria Regulatory and Supervisory Guidelines for Bureau De Change Operations in Nigeria 2024, issued under BOFIA 2020 section 56, supersede the Revised Operational Guidelines for Bureau De Change in Nigeria issued in November 2015 and related circulars and directives, effective 3 June 2024.
reviews.rationale: CBN BDC Guidelines 2024 circular supersession limb supported: 2024 Guidelines issued under BOFIA s.56 supersede the November 2015 Revised Operational Guidelines and related circulars/directives, effective 3 June 2024. Special review closed. Current-vs-superseded framework claim only — does not resurrect 2015 operational rules and does not project BDC retail permissions into corporate/import/investment classes beyond this instrument.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act establishes an Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market, and the Central Bank of Nigeria may, with the approval of the Minister, issue guidelines from time to time to regulate the procedures for transactions in the Market and other matters appropriate for the Market’s effective operation.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA s.1(1)-(2) supported: Autonomous Foreign Exchange Market established; CBN may, with Minister approval, issue guidelines regulating Market procedures and effective operation. Special review closed. Regulatory-authority proposition only — does not establish that CBN administratively sets every transaction rate, and does not establish a managed-float or floating taxonomy.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria FX Structure and Management page, Nigeria’s foreign exchange market framework has shifted from a tightly regulated, administratively controlled system to a largely market driven regime.
reviews.reviewed_text: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria FX Structure and Management page, over the years the framework has shifted from a tightly regulated, administratively controlled system to a largely market driven regime.
reviews.rationale: CBN Structure page operating language supported. Bounded reviewed_text restores the source 'Over the years' framing. Special review closed. Official operating description 'largely market driven regime' retained — not converted into formal floating, free-float, or managed-float taxonomy, and not read as absence of CBN regulation or intervention.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Under the Central Bank of Nigeria FX Structure and Management page’s 2016–2023 period heading, the Central Bank in June 2016 adopted a managed floating exchange rate regime and introduced the Investors’ and Exporters’ Foreign Exchange Window as a market driven platform for eligible FX transactions.
reviews.rationale: CBN Structure page 2016–2023 period heading historical posture supported: June 2016 adoption of a managed floating exchange rate regime and introduction of the I&E window. Special review closed. Temporal scope remains historical (2016–2023 heading). Does not establish that Nigeria currently operates a managed floating regime under the page's 2023-Date architecture.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: On 14 June 2023, the Central Bank of Nigeria introduced a willing buyer, willing seller model for the conduct of transactions in the domestic foreign exchange market.
reviews.rationale: CBN Structure page 14 June 2023 willing buyer, willing seller model introduction supported. Special review closed. Official operating formulation retained — not normalized into floating, free-floating, or unrestricted-market taxonomy.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Under the Central Bank of Nigeria’s 14 June 2023 foreign-exchange reform described on the FX Structure and Management page, the multiplicity of foreign exchange windows was eliminated and market segments were consolidated into a single framework now referred to as the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market.
reviews.reviewed_text: Under the Central Bank of Nigeria’s 14 June 2023 foreign-exchange reform described on the FX Structure and Management page, the multiplicity of foreign exchange windows was eliminated, and all market segments were consolidated into a single framework now referred to as the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM).
reviews.rationale: NFEM consolidation limb supported. Bounded reviewed_text restores source 'all market segments' wording and the NFEM acronym. Special review closed. Official-window consolidation only — does not establish that any parallel/unofficial market disappeared, that every exchange rate in Nigeria is identical, that no segmentation of any kind remains, or that no regulatory control remains.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria FX Structure and Management page, the 14 June 2023 reform strengthened the role of demand and supply in the exchange rate formation process under the willing buyer, willing seller model.
reviews.rationale: CBN Structure page demand-and-supply role in exchange-rate formation under the 14 June 2023 WBWS model supported. Special review closed. Does not establish free-float taxonomy, absence of intervention, or duplicate Hardening III FEMMPA s.9 mutually agreed transaction-rate claim (NG-BIZ-03) — this is a macro formation-language proposition from the Structure page.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Central Bank of Nigeria Monetary Policy reforms materials state that foreign-exchange market reforms have been ongoing to drive the unification of multiple FX windows under a transparent willing buyer, willing seller system, and that the Bank introduced the FXCode and the Bloomberg B-Matching platform to improve transparency and price discovery and implemented the Electronic Foreign Exchange Matching System to ensure transparency, fair and efficient FX trading, minimise counterparty risk, and ensure compliance with CBN regulations.
reviews.rationale: CBN Monetary Policy reforms FX package supported: ongoing unification under transparent WBWS; FXCode and Bloomberg B-Matching for transparency/price discovery; EFEMS for transparent, fair, efficient trading, counterparty-risk minimisation, and CBN-regulation compliance. Special review closed. Reform-package / infrastructure description — EFEMS limbs are infrastructure and compliance, not customer entitlement, free-float taxonomy, or proof CBN never intervenes. Later Adoption Gate should avoid cloning already-governed H3 EFEMS channel claims without a distinct macro need.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria Foreign Exchange Market page, adoption of a willing buyer, willing seller model for trade transactions unified the foreign exchange market in 2023, abolished FX market segmentation, and collapsed previously existing segments into the Investors’ and Exporters’ window, now renamed the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market.
reviews.reviewed_text: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria Foreign Exchange Market page, the Central Bank of Nigeria adopted a willing buyer, willing seller model for trade transactions, therefore unifying the foreign exchange market in 2023. This led to the abolishment of FX market segmentation, and collapse of the previously existing segments into the Investors’ and Exporters’ (I&E) window, now renamed Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM).
reviews.rationale: FX Market page 2023 unification/NFEM rename supported. Bounded reviewed_text restores source 'for trade transactions' / 'therefore unifying' structure. Special review closed. Institutional window consolidation and rename only — not every rate identical, not parallel market abolished, and not absence of regulatory control.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: On the Central Bank of Nigeria exchange-rates page, the NFEM rate is derived at volume-weighted average and stands as the official exchange rate for the day.
reviews.rationale: CBN exchange-rates page footnote supported: NFEM rate derived at volume-weighted average and stands as the official exchange rate for the day. Special review closed. Published official/reference-series mechanics only — not equated to every individual transaction rate, not a fixed exchange-rate regime, and not a mandatory transaction-rate rule.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria EFEMS FAQs, EFEMS is expected to promote a market-driven exchange rate, meaning rates will reflect actual market conditions.
reviews.rationale: EFEMS FAQ 'expected to promote a market-driven exchange rate' limb supported with exact official term retained. Special review closed. Expectation / operating objective for EFEMS pricing — not free float, laissez-faire FX, absence of CBN regulation, absence of intervention, customer entitlement, or formal regime taxonomy.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria EFEMS FAQs, real-time rates and other key data from EFEMS will be published on the selected platform and CBN official websites, and those rates would serve as a reference rate for USDNGN, with the computation methodology to be communicated to market participants.
reviews.rationale: EFEMS FAQ reference-rate publication limb supported: published EFEMS rates would serve as USDNGN reference rate; methodology to be communicated. Special review closed. Reference-rate mechanics distinct from individual transaction rates and from a fixed exchange-rate regime.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: According to the Central Bank of Nigeria EFEMS FAQs, the Central Bank, in collaboration with the Financial Markets Dealers Association, will regulate the EFEMS system and publish guidelines, rules, and real-time data to ensure compliance with the Nigerian FX Code and the revised Market Operating Guidelines for the Nigeria Foreign Exchange Market.
reviews.rationale: EFEMS FAQ CBN(+FMDA) regulatory role supported: regulate the system; publish guidelines/rules/real-time data for FX Code and revised Market Operating Guidelines compliance. Special review closed. Regulatory/supervisory proposition only — not managed-float taxonomy and not that CBN administratively sets every transaction rate.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The Central Bank of Nigeria FX Structure and Management page describes the June 2016 adoption of a managed floating exchange rate regime under the heading 2016–2023: Market Deepening, Liquidity Enhancement, and Investor Confidence.
reviews.rationale: CBN Structure page temporal scoping supported: June 2016 managed floating adoption is described under the heading 2016–2023: Market Deepening, Liquidity Enhancement, and Investor Confidence. Special review closed. Historical/period-scoped only — does not establish current-rule managed float and must not leak into 2023-Date public-field drafting without Adoption Gate temporal judgment.
